251.explanation: An external examination by regulators or their agents measures the company's policies against the external requirements they impose. An internal audit is run by the organization itself and does not show how regulators assess compliance.

252.explanation: Isolating the critical end-of-life system in its own VLAN limits exposure while it keeps processing transactions. Decommissioning would remove a business-critical system, and HIDS or encryption do not address unpatchable OS flaws.

253.explanation: Recurring vulnerability scans show whether patches were applied and which vulnerabilities remain, tracking patch status. Scans do not hunt for active attackers or discover shadow IT cloud deployments.

254.explanation: Insiders already have access, so copying data to unauthorized removable media is the most common exfiltration vector. Spear phishing and typosquatting are used by external actors to gain access.

255.explanation: A spoofed HR message with links pointing to non-company sites is phishing, a social engineering vector. Business email compromise would involve a hijacked legitimate account, which is not indicated.

256.explanation: An accurate asset inventory lists every system and its software, so all systems needing the patch can be identified. Network enumeration is a point-in-time discovery activity, not a maintained record.

257.explanation: Uploaded PDFs can carry malware, so malware detection on a UTM inspects files before they reach the site. A WAF blocking command injection targets web requests, not malicious file content.

258.explanation: Version control tracks each revision of a document, recording what changed and when. The other options are not formal processes for managing revisions.

259.explanation: Trusted devices let users log in seamlessly from any location using equipment they already have, while blocking unknown devices used in takeovers. Smart cards require extra hardware, and geotagging would hinder a globally distributed workforce.

260.explanation: A hash of the final build lets anyone verify the software has not been altered, since any change produces a different hash. Encryption protects confidentiality, not integrity.

261.explanation: SAML is the standard federation protocol for extending existing enterprise SSO to a cloud SaaS application. RADIUS and EAP are used for network access authentication, not web application SSO.

262.explanation: Ignoring a certificate warning on public Wi-Fi suggests an attacker intercepted the session in an on-path attack and captured card details. A replay attack resends captured data but does not explain the certificate warning.

263.explanation: With only one ISP connection, an outage there takes the network down regardless of switch redundancy, making it a single point of failure. MTBF and RPO do not describe the lack of a redundant link.

264.explanation: VLAN segmentation is a technical control, and it compensates for the risk of an end-of-life server that cannot be patched. It is not physical or managerial, and it does not detect or correct events.
flags: Source formatting: options F and G were merged on one line in the source; split into F. Technical and G. Deterrent (7 options).

265.explanation: Since the attacker can already log in to the stolen device, remote wipe through MDM is the way to remove company data from it. Full disk encryption offers no protection once the device is unlocked with valid credentials.

266.explanation: Code obfuscation makes source or compiled code hard to understand, which hinders reverse engineering. Digital signing proves origin and integrity but does not hide how the code works.

267.explanation: Longer passwords and a special-character requirement increase complexity, making passwords harder to guess. Changing the hashing algorithm protects stored hashes but does not stop users choosing guessable passwords.

268.explanation: An inbound external connection on an uncommon port after installing untrusted software indicates a backdoor allowing remote access. A keylogger captures keystrokes and would typically send data outbound rather than accept connections.

269.explanation: An IaaS provider can supply scalable compute and storage on resilient infrastructure, meeting all three requirements. Dual PDUs address only the power circuit requirement, not storage scalability or memory baseline.

270.explanation: A DNS sinkhole returns a controlled address for known-malicious domains, capturing and blocking that traffic. Luring attackers away from production resources describes a honeypot, not a sinkhole.

271.explanation: S/MIME digital signatures bind a message to the sender's private key, providing non-repudiation and integrity. Signatures do not by themselves block phishing or improve delivery.

272.explanation: IoT devices have limited CPU, memory and power, so cryptography must be chosen to fit those resource constraints. Bandwidth and TLS version are secondary to whether the device can run the algorithm at all.

273.explanation: A SOC 2 Type 2 report is an independent attestation that controls operated effectively over a period of time, such as six months. NIST CSF is a framework, not proof of control operation, and a vulnerability report is a point-in-time view.

274.explanation: Segregation of duties prevents one person from completing a sensitive task alone, stopping fraud before it happens. Auditing, log correlation and alerts are detective controls.

275.explanation: Blocking the URL shortener domain at the web proxy stops users from following any of the links regardless of subject line or eventual destination. Subject-line blocklists fail because subjects vary, and sinkholing a dead domain does little.

276.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of real-world adversary tactics and techniques, with mitigations mapped to them. CVSS scores vulnerability severity and does not describe adversary behavior.

277.explanation: Certificate errors followed by disconnection indicate the client does not trust the LDAPS server's certificate, so it must be added to the local truststore. The port is clearly open since the TLS handshake starts.

278.explanation: Telnet sends credentials in cleartext, so a packet capture tool could easily capture the administrator's password. Spraying or dictionary attacks are unnecessary when the password is exposed on the wire.

279.explanation: SSH provides encrypted remote command-line access and is the secure replacement for Telnet. RDP provides graphical remote desktop access and is not the direct replacement for Telnet server management.

280.explanation: A wildcard certificate covers all subdomains of a domain with one certificate, reducing cost. Self-signed certificates are not trusted by external clients, and client and code-signing certificates serve other purposes.

281.explanation: Nessus is a vulnerability scanner that reports open insecure ports and legacy protocols across servers. Wireshark captures traffic but does not audit server configurations.

282.explanation: The capture shows IPv6 traffic carried inside IPv4 (protocol 41), so the data was hidden by encapsulation/tunneling. There is no evidence of altered MAC addresses or data concealed inside media files.

283.explanation: Serverless architecture lets code be deployed without provisioning or managing servers, reducing deployment time and cost. Virtual machines and private clouds still require infrastructure management.

284.explanation: A password cracker needs to read /etc/shadow, which stores the password hashes, so the permission error points to that tool. A file integrity monitor checks for changes rather than attempting to read hashes for cracking.

285.explanation: RTP, SIP, H.323 and SRTP are signaling and media protocols used by VoIP. RTOS, SoC and HVAC are embedded or specialized systems unrelated to these protocols.

286.explanation: Whaling is phishing aimed at senior executives such as the CEO. Spear phishing targets specific individuals generally, while whaling specifically targets executives.

287.explanation: PAM software brokers and vaults privileged credentials, granting monitored access to critical systems without revealing passwords. SSO and SAML simplify authentication but do not hide privileged credentials.

288.explanation: A captive portal requiring acceptance of terms and conditions puts visitors on notice of acceptable use, addressing the legal concern. RADIUS and 802.1X authenticate devices but do not set usage terms for guests.

289.explanation: Lighting deters intruders and helps detect them, while sensors detect intrusions and their presence discourages attempts. Signage and fencing deter but do not detect activity.

290.explanation: A load balancer distributes customer requests across servers to keep the application available during peak usage. Cloud backups and geographic dispersal support recovery, not load handling.

291.explanation: Code signing lets users verify the software came from the author and has not been repackaged with malware. Input validation and fuzzing improve code quality but do not prove a download's integrity.

292.explanation: Changes to a released design should go through the change control process for approval, impact analysis and documentation. A design review already occurred when the issues were identified.

293.explanation: The mimikatz sekurlsa::pth command uses an NTLM hash of the localadmin account, which is a pass-the-hash attack using a shared account. Mimikatz is a dropped tool, not a living-off-the-land binary, and no social engineering is shown.

294.explanation: OWASP publishes resources such as the Top 10 that describe the most common web application exploitation methods. CVE lists individual vulnerabilities rather than common exploitation methods.

295.explanation: Unused, non-compliant desktops add risk without business value, so decommissioning them is the best recommendation. Patching or isolating would keep unneeded assets on the network.

296.explanation: Sanitization securely wipes data in a repeatable way while leaving the drive usable. Degaussing destroys magnetic media's usability, and formatting does not reliably remove data.

297.explanation: Time-based tokens (TOTP) work across SaaS and internal apps, run on any device, and generate codes without network connectivity. SMS verification requires cellular service, and biometrics depend on specific device hardware.

298.explanation: A simulated phishing campaign is a standard component of a security awareness program alongside posters and training. Password policies and risk assessments are not awareness activities.

299.explanation: An unauthenticated upload page allowed a web shell to be deployed, which then runs an unknown process and calls out to a low-reputation IP. A worm would spread to other systems, and no exposed RDP port is indicated.

300.explanation: SCAP automates configuration and vulnerability checks against standards; it does not by itself analyze a supply chain. A third-party penetration test is the listed independent assessment that can examine supply chain exposure. The source key gives SCAP.
flags: Possible wrong answer: SCAP is a configuration-compliance standard, not a supply chain analysis method; a third-party penetration test is the closer fit for SY0-701 vendor/supply chain assessment.
